pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Sound Travels Through Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 4 Sound):** Pupils should recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear. (Media include solids, liquids and gases; the string-telephone is a canonical vehicle.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-PS4-1, partial):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-1]." This establishes that sound is vibration of materials, which underpins travel-through-a-medium, but NGSS does not give an elementary performance expectation for sound requiring a medium / not travelling through a vacuum — that is treated at MS-PS4. This topic is therefore UK-anchored, with 1-PS4-1 as the nearest elementary bridge and the vacuum idea flagged as a later (MS) extension.

- **Operational details:** Children learn that a sound is a vibration that has to be PASSED ON through some material — solid, liquid or gas — to reach the ear; it cannot travel through nothing (a vacuum). Build from the prerequisite that vibrations make sound: now the vibration is handed from particle to particle across a medium. Canonical experiences: the string/cup telephone (voice vibrates the cup → vibrations run along the taut string → second cup vibrates the air to the ear — and go slack and it stops); tapping a table and hearing it louder with an ear pressed to the wood (solid); hearing sounds while underwater or clicking spoons in a bowl of water (liquid); everyday hearing through air (gas). The pattern to draw out: sound needs 'stuff' to travel through, and it can travel through solids and liquids as well as air — deliberately over-sampling non-air media because children default to 'sound only travels through air.' The vacuum idea is introduced conceptually (bell-in-a-jar demo/video; 'no air in space, so no sound') as the boundary case that proves a medium is required.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can give examples of sound travelling through a solid, a liquid and a gas, explain the string-telephone chain (vibration passed along the string), and state that sound needs a material to travel through so it cannot travel through empty space. Mastery is the medium-required generalisation across all three states of matter — not a particle/pressure-wave model (Tier C, MS-PS4).
bestPractices: Deliberately over-sample non-air media — have children hear sound through a solid (ear to the desk) and a liquid (spoons clicked in water, or heads underwater) — to directly confront the 'sound only travels through air' default.
Use the string/cup telephone as the anchor: make it work with a taut string and fail with a slack one, so the child sees a sound needs a continuous MATERIAL path to travel along.
Draw out the generalisation explicitly — 'solids, liquids AND gases' — rather than leaving air as the implicit norm, and record examples of each state.
Introduce the vacuum as the boundary case (bell-in-a-jar demo/video, 'space is silent') so 'a medium is required' is proven by its absence, not just asserted.
Connect back to the prerequisite (vibrations make sound) by describing travel as the vibration being 'handed on' through the material to the ear.
keyRepresentations: String/cup telephone — the canonical model of a vibration travelling along a taut material path (works taut, stops slack).
Ear-to-the-desk / tap-the-table — sound travelling (louder) through a solid.
Spoons or a sound source in a bowl of water / underwater listening — sound travelling through a liquid.
Bell-in-a-vacuum-jar (demo or video) — sound fading to silence as the air is removed, showing a medium is required.
A source–medium–ear line: buzzing source → the material in between → the ear, with the medium as the swappable middle link.
commonMisconceptions: Believing sound only travels through air — not recognising it also travels through solids and liquids (often better).
Thinking sound can travel through empty space / a vacuum (e.g. hearing explosions in space films), i.e. that no material is needed.
Assuming a solid wall BLOCKS sound entirely rather than transmitting it (confusing muffling/absorption with 'can't pass through').
Treating the string telephone as carrying the voice as air INSIDE the string, rather than the string itself vibrating along its length.
Thinking sound gets to the ear by the air 'moving across' as a wind/breeze rather than a vibration being passed along in place.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9 (UK Year 4 Sound; NGSS 1-PS4-1 as the nearest elementary bridge, with the vacuum idea flagged as a later MS-PS4 extension): children learn that a sound is a vibration that must be passed on through some material - solid, liquid or gas - to reach the ear, and that it cannot travel through empty space (a vacuum). The target is the medium-required generalisation across all three states of matter, NOT a particle/pressure-wave model. Teaching deliberately over-samples non-air media (ear to a solid, listening through water) to confront the common 'sound only travels through air' default, uses the string/cup telephone to show sound needs a continuous material path, and introduces the vacuum as the boundary case that proves a medium is required.

activities.title: Pick-a-medium sound bench (on-screen): swap the material between source and ear
feedback: If a learner predicts the solid or water will block the sound, have them also test it first-hand (ear on a desk while a friend taps the far end; listening to spoons clicked in water): solids and liquids carry sound, often better than air.
If a learner expects sound to still arrive across the emptied/vacuum gap, point out there is nothing there to carry the vibration from one side to the other, so it falls silent.

If a learner thinks the sound reaches the ear by air 'blowing across' like a wind or breeze, clarify that the vibration is passed on through the material, which stays roughly where it is - the material does not travel to the ear like a draught.
Reinforce by naming the chain: source vibrates, the vibration is handed across the material in between, and that reaches the ear - the material in the middle is the swappable link.
activities.rationale: Making the medium the child's choice, with a predict-then-test step, turns 'a medium is required' into something the learner causes and observes rather than is told, and directly targets the air-only default by letting them experience sound through solids and liquids. The vacuum-removal step is only achievable in the on-screen interactive (or, physically, via a bell-in-a-jar demonstration), since a real vacuum cannot be made at a bench. An optional travelling-vibration animation rippling across the gap can make the 'handed on' mechanism visible; this is an illustrative aid, not a required mechanism. The on-screen sandbox and the separate hands-on listening experiences complement each other.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear.

Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (not only air); children commonly hold an 'air-only' misconception, so teaching should deliberately include hearing sound through solids and liquids, and use the string telephone to show vibrations passing along a material path.
learnerActions: Open the on-screen pick-a-medium interactive: a buzzing source (e.g. a bell or buzzer) on one side, an 'ear' on the other, and a gap you fill with a chosen material.
Before each trial, predict out loud: 'Will I hear the buzz through this material - strongly, faintly, or not at all?' and say why.

Drop air, then water, then wood, then a brick wall into the gap, and each time observe/listen whether the sound gets through and how its character changes (e.g. it can arrive strongly when the source and ear are in contact with a solid, and is still audible through water; a thick wall can also muffle sound that starts in the air).

Then choose 'remove everything' to empty the gap into a vacuum on-screen, and observe that the sound cuts to silence because the vibration has nothing to travel through. (This on-screen removal is what makes the vacuum case testable - you cannot make a real vacuum at a desk, so the physical counterpart is the bell-in-a-jar demonstration.)

State in your own words what the model showed (and what the real listening and bell-in-a-jar evidence supports): sound needs 'stuff' (a material) to travel through, and travels through solids and liquids as well as air, but not through empty space.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound is a vibration that must be handed on through a material to reach the ear; solids and liquids carry it as well as air, and when the material is removed the sound stops - so a medium is required.

activities.title: String telephone: taut carries well, slack carries poorly
feedback: If a learner thinks the voice travels as air moving inside the string, clarify that the string itself vibrates along its length - it is the solid material carrying the vibration, not air inside it.

If a learner is unsure why slack weakens it, explain that a loose string flops and does not pass the vibration along well, while a tight string does; if the string were cut, there would be no material path at all, like emptying the gap on the bench.
activities.rationale: The taut-works-well/slack-works-poorly contrast shows that the vibrating string itself carries the sound, addressing the misconception that the string carries air inside it. Ordering the chain supports the DfE evidence point of describing how a string telephone works.
sourceClaims: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (not only air); children commonly hold an 'air-only' misconception, so teaching should deliberately include hearing sound through solids and liquids, and use the string telephone to show vibrations passing along a material path.
learnerActions: Make a cup-and-string telephone and speak into one cup while a partner listens at the other with the string pulled taut.
Then let the string go slack and try again, noticing that the voice becomes much fainter or cannot be heard.
Explain the chain in order: your voice vibrates the first cup, the vibration runs along the taut string, it vibrates the second cup, which vibrates the air to your partner's ear.

Explain why it fades when slack: the vibration travels along the string best when the string is pulled tight; a loose, floppy string does not pass the vibration on well, even though it still joins the cups.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound travels along a material path; the taut string itself vibrates along its length to carry the voice, while a slack string passes the vibration on poorly, so the sound becomes much fainter or is lost.

activities.title: Ear to the desk and listening through water (first-hand media)
feedback: If a learner says you only hear the tap through cracks/gaps, have them press against a solid surface with no gaps and tap the far end: the material itself carries the vibration through its body.
If a learner is surprised the solid sounds louder/clearer, confirm that solids often carry sound better than air (this depends on the material and setup).
activities.rationale: Deliberately over-sampling non-air media with first-hand experience confronts the 'air-only' default and the related idea that solids simply block sound rather than transmit it. Recording one example per state supports the explicit 'solids, liquids AND gases' generalisation.
sourceClaims: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (not only air); children commonly hold an 'air-only' misconception, so teaching should deliberately include hearing sound through solids and liquids, and use the string telephone to show vibrations passing along a material path.
learnerActions: Press your ear flat on a table and have a friend tap the far end of the table (not through the air) - listen and compare with hearing the tap through the air alone.
Click two spoons together under the water in a bowl with your ear pressed against the side of the bowl, or listen to sounds while underwater, and notice the sound still reaches you through the water.
For each, say which state of matter carried the sound (solid, liquid) and record an example of sound travelling through a solid, a liquid and a gas.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound travels through solids and liquids as well as air - sometimes more clearly - so sound is not limited to air.

activities.title: Why is space silent? The vacuum boundary case
feedback: If a learner says sound still carries across empty space (as in films/games), connect back to the jar: as air is removed the sound dies because there is nothing left to carry it.
If a learner says 'space is too far' for sound, clarify the reason is the missing material, not distance.
activities.rationale: Introducing the vacuum as the boundary case lets 'a medium is required' be shown by its absence rather than just asserted, and directly tackles the film/game-driven misconception that sound crosses empty space. An in-role astronaut conversation is a motivating curiosity hook or reflective extension; it surfaces reasoning but should accompany, not replace, the material-swapping experiences.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear.
learnerActions: Watch or discuss a bell-in-a-jar demonstration/video where the sound fades as the air is pumped out.
Discuss whether the BANG of an explosion in a space film is realistic, and explain your reasoning.

Optionally, interview an astronaut in role (or imagine one): ask what they hear outside the craft, why they use radios, and why a wrench tapped against the outside of the hull is silent to a colleague floating nearby in space without touching the craft.
State the conclusion: there is no air (no material) in space, so there is nothing to carry the vibration - space is silent, which shows sound needs a medium.
activities.intendedInsight: A vacuum has no material to carry vibrations, so sound cannot cross it - the absence of sound in space shows that a medium is required.

activities.title: Media, vacuum and the telephone chain: consolidation check
feedback: Correct responses: (a) yes - solids carry sound, though a door may make a voice sound muffled; (b) yes - liquids carry sound; (c) no - a vacuum has no material to carry the vibration, so it is silent.
If a learner marks the door or water as blocking sound, revisit the first-hand solid/liquid listening activities.
If a learner marks the vacuum as carrying sound, revisit the bell-in-a-jar boundary case.
activities.rationale: These checks confirm and consolidate the generalisation and map onto the DfE assessment-shaped evidence points. Sorting, sequencing and choosing can confirm and check the generalisation, but on their own they do not let a child discover the medium-required boundary first-hand, so they work best after the material-swapping and vacuum experiences.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear.

Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (not only air); children commonly hold an 'air-only' misconception, so teaching should deliberately include hearing sound through solids and liquids, and use the string telephone to show vibrations passing along a material path.
learnerActions: Sort scenarios into 'sound reaches the ear' vs 'no sound' (e.g. tap heard through a wall, voices underwater -> reaches; explosion in airless space, bell in an emptied jar -> no sound).
Put the string-telephone chain in order: mouth speaks -> first cup vibrates -> string vibrates -> second cup vibrates -> air to the ear.
Answer 'why is space silent?' and justify choosing 'sound needs a material to travel through' over 'space is too far away'.

Answer the three-way prompt: would a voice carry (a) through a solid wooden door, (b) through the water in a swimming pool, (c) across empty airless space like on the Moon? Give yes/yes/no and explain each.
activities.intendedInsight: Across solid, liquid and vacuum cases, only the medium-required idea gives the correct pattern (yes/yes/no); space is silent because of missing material, not distance.

constraints: Target the medium-required generalisation across solids, liquids and gases; do NOT require a particle/pressure-wave model, which belongs to a later (MS-PS4) stage.

The vacuum/no-sound-in-space idea is a conceptual boundary case at this level, introduced via on-screen interactive or bell-in-a-jar demo/video and reasoning, not a formal elementary performance expectation (NGSS places it at middle school).

A real vacuum cannot be produced by children at a desk; the material-removal/vacuum step belongs to the on-screen interactive or the bell-in-a-jar demonstration, while ear-to-desk and water listening are the genuine first-hand experiences.

Sort/sequence/choose checks can confirm and check the generalisation but do not let a child discover the medium-required boundary first-hand; use them after experiences that let the learner swap or remove the material.

A static labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal of the chain (cup, taut string, cup, ear) can teach the vocabulary and the pathway, but does not let the child remove the medium and hear silence; treat it as a companion, not the primary build.

An astronaut dialogue is a curiosity hook/reflective extension that surfaces reasoning; pair it with, don't replace, the hands-on material-swapping, since the medium-required idea is well shown by changing materials.

Illustrative animations (a ripple travelling across the gap) are optional aids to make the 'handed on' mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms and the real learning is the material-swap outcome.

Use the string-telephone taut/slack contrast to show that the taut, vibrating string carries the sound (a slack string still joins the cups but passes the vibration on poorly); clarify the string itself vibrates, rather than carrying air inside it.
A 3D scene is not needed at this level; the concept is well captured by a source-medium-ear line. Spatial 3D (e.g. echoes bouncing in a room) is only relevant much later.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assumes a bell-in-a-jar demo/video and underwater/through-solid listening produce clear, expected results; actual audibility depends on setup and materials. Present these as observations to test, and do not promise a specific outcome regardless of conditions. The on-screen interactive outcomes are designer-controlled models of these expected results.

The original row framed dialogue as something that 'cannot deliver' the medium-required idea and a static image as unable to 'teach the medium-required causal boundary'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the evidence cited and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Genuine objective limit retained: confirm-only sort/sequence/choose tasks do not by themselves elicit the learner's independent discovery of the boundary.
The claim that solids carry sound 'often faster and better than through air' is broadly true for many solids but is material-dependent; stated here as 'often' rather than universal.

The original's 'pick-a-medium bench' is a coded 2D interactive; it is framed here as an on-screen interactive with the bell-in-a-jar as its physical counterpart, since children cannot make a real vacuum at a desk.

The original pedagogy's wind/breeze misconception (sound reaching the ear by air moving across rather than a vibration passed along in place) was not explicitly addressed in the candidate's activities; a feedback item has been added to activity 1 (pick-a-medium bench) to preserve it.

assess.poeTask: Predict: if you press your ear flat against the table while a friend taps the FAR end of the table (not through the air), will you hear it clearly, faintly, or not at all? Say why first, then try it and explain what carried the sound.
probeDeeper: How does a string telephone work — what carries your voice from one cup to the other?
In films, explosions in space go BANG. Is that realistic? Why or why not?
Press your ear flat on the table and have a friend tap the far end — can you hear it? What is carrying the sound?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) The wooden door: yes — solids carry sound (often better than air). (b) The water: yes — liquids carry sound. (c) Empty airless space: NO — sound needs a material (a medium) to travel through, and there is nothing there to carry the vibrations, so it is silent. Sound is not limited to air, but it cannot cross a vacuum.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound only through air: 'you can only hear through air; a solid or water blocks the sound'
errorPatterns.nextMove: First-hand hearing through a solid (ear on the table, tap the far end) and through water; sound travels through solids and liquids, often faster and better than through air.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sound only travels through air, so the door and the water block it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the voice won't carry through the door or the water

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound travels through empty space: 'you'd still hear it across airless space / space isn't silent' (from films and games)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sound needs a medium; a bell in a jar goes silent as the air is pumped out; space is silent because there is nothing there to carry the vibration.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — sound would still carry across empty space with no air.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says voices or explosions carry across a vacuum

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound gets through only via gaps: 'you hear through the door because of cracks around it, not through the wood'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Press an ear to a solid surface with no gaps and tap the far end — the material itself carries the vibration from particle to particle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says sound passes the door only through gaps, not by vibrating the solid material

responseLevels.gap: Says sound travels only through air (door and water block it), or that sound carries across empty airless space.
responseLevels.full: States that sound needs a material medium and travels through solids, liquids and gases but NOT a vacuum; gives the yes/yes/no answer; and explains the string telephone and why space is silent.
responseLevels.partial: Knows sound travels through more than air (e.g. water or solids) but is unsure about the vacuum case, or thinks sound crosses a solid only through gaps.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children want to hear each other. Would a voice carry to the other's ear (a) through a solid wooden door, (b) through the water in a swimming pool, and (c) across empty space with NO air at all, like on the Moon? For each one, say whether sound gets through, and explain why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The prompt contrasts three media — solid, liquid, and vacuum — in one question. A child who thinks 'sound only travels through air' wrongly says the solid and the water block it; a child who thinks space carries sound wrongly says the vacuum works. Only the correct medium concept produces yes/yes/no. The vacuum case is the sharpest tell because films and games teach the opposite.
